name: Myofunctional therapy
lead: Orofacial myofunctional therapy (OMT) is a program of exercises for the tongue, lips, cheeks and throat muscles, used clinically for conditions such as obstructive sleep apnea, tongue dysfunction and open bite [1][4]. People in looksmaxxing communities discuss it alongside tongue posture and mewing as a route to better jaw position, a clearer breathing pattern and a more defined lower face, though what is studied is function rather than looks [9][10].

A systematic review and meta-analysis of myofunctional therapy for obstructive sleep apnea examined polysomnographic, snoring and sleepiness outcomes in children and adults [1]. Further studies examine its use alongside CPAP, in children with sleep-disordered breathing, and in orthodontic cases [3][5][6][7]. Published research concerns airway and oral function; no trial located for this entry has tested facial appearance.

paras: Therapy programs promote changes in the musculature of the upper airway and mouth, and published reviews summarize the programs used and their possible mechanisms [4]. Typical programs combine tongue-strengthening and positioning exercises, lip and cheek muscle training, retraining of swallowing, and a shift towards nasal breathing, usually supervised over a series of sessions with home practice [4][7].
Outcome measures in studies include tongue elevation strength, resting tongue posture, swallowing pattern, snoring, daytime sleepiness and the apnea-hypopnea index (AHI) from sleep studies [1][3][7].

A 2015 systematic review and meta-analysis pooled studies in children and adults [1]. In nine adult studies (120 patients) the authors report AHI falling from about 24.5 to 12.3 events per hour, a rise in lowest oxygen saturation, less snoring and lower Epworth sleepiness scores; in two pediatric studies (25 patients) AHI also decreased, and children who continued therapy after surgery stayed free of apnea over four years compared with controls [1]. The authors estimated reductions of roughly 50 percent in adults and 62 percent in children [1].

A European Respiratory Society guideline on non-CPAP therapies for sleep apnoea, developed with the GRADE approach, includes myofunctional therapy among seven options it addresses, alongside surgery, mandibular advancement devices, hypoglossal nerve stimulation, carbonic anhydrase inhibitors and positional therapy [2]. A 2018 review describes the programs and proposed mechanisms [4].

A randomized trial registered as NCT01289405 assigned 100 men with obstructive sleep apnea to placebo therapy, myofunctional therapy, CPAP, or CPAP plus myofunctional therapy, with assessments after three months [3]. All treated groups had lower sleepiness and snoring, with the largest AHI reduction in the CPAP group. The myofunctional and combined groups improved tongue and soft-palate muscle strength relative to placebo, and the combined group used CPAP more than the CPAP-only group [3].

Studies have examined myofunctional reeducation in children with sleep-disordered breathing [5][6]. A pilot randomized trial of 22 children aged about 7 to 10 with anterior open bite and an immature swallowing pattern reported that OMT changed tongue elevation strength, resting tongue posture and tongue position during swallowing, with better tooth contact six months later; speech articulation did not change [7]. A further study examined relapse of open bites treated with appliances with and without therapy [8].

sections.h: Relation to mewing and tongue posture
paras: Mewing is named after British orthodontist John Mew, who developed the idea with his son Mike Mew as part of orthotropics, and holds that tongue-to-palate posture reshapes the jaws [10]. Wikipedia reports that interest rose on search and social platforms from January 2019, especially in looksmaxxing communities [10]. It describes mewing as unproven, reports that researchers have found no credible evidence for orthotropics, and notes that Mike Mew was struck off the UK dental register in 2024; the American Association of Orthodontists states there is no evidence mewing improves the jaw [10].

Clinical OMT is a separate, therapist-led discipline with its own research base in airway and swallowing function. Looksmaxxers sometimes group the two together, and some commentators distinguish them: OMT studies assess tongue function and breathing, whereas mewing claims concern bone structure [9][10].

On looksmax.org, users have asked whether jaw-growth devices and myofunctional exercises are pseudoscience, after a consultation that likened them to mewing [9]. The poster described clinicians claiming a few millimetres of forward movement through exercises and a device, linked to posture [9].

The studies cited do not report notable adverse effects from the exercises. Sleep apnea is a medical condition, and the guidelines cited place myofunctional therapy among several treatments to be chosen with a clinician [2][3].

Studies cited above cover sleep apnea, CPAP adherence, pediatric sleep-disordered breathing and open bite [1][3][5][6][7][8]. Reported results include lower AHI and snoring in adults and children, higher tongue strength and CPAP adherence in a randomized trial, and changes in tongue posture in children with open bite [1][3][7]. None located for this entry assessed facial appearance as an outcome.

timeline.event: Trial NCT01289405 of myofunctional therapy and CPAP in sleep apnea is registered; results published in 2017 [3].
Systematic review and meta-analysis reports reduced AHI after myofunctional therapy in adults and children [1].
Pilot randomized trial in children with anterior open bite and tongue dysfunction is published [7].
Review focusing on myofunctional therapy in obstructive sleep apnea is published [4].
Public interest in mewing and tongue posture rises sharply on social media [10].
European Respiratory Society publishes a guideline on non-CPAP therapies for obstructive sleep apnoea, including myofunctional therapy [2].
Mike Mew is struck off the UK dental register, according to Wikipedia [10].

lore.intro: Forum discussion links myofunctional therapy to tongue posture and jaw exercises [9].

claims.claim: Myofunctional exercises can move a recessed jaw forward
claims.believers: A user reports a consultation in which clinicians described gaining several millimetres of forward movement through exercises and a device, linking it to posture [9].
claims.experts: Published studies address airway and function outcomes; no study located tested jaw position change for appearance [1][4].

claims.claim: Myofunctional therapy and mewing are the same thing
claims.believers: Users and some clinicians compare the two because both focus on tongue posture [9].
claims.experts: Wikipedia describes mewing as an orthotropics practice with no credible evidence for jaw reshaping, whereas OMT studies measure airway and tongue function [10][1].

claims.claim: Tongue exercises reduce snoring and sleep apnea
claims.believers: Practitioners present the exercises as a non-surgical option for snoring and mild sleep apnea [4].
claims.experts: A meta-analysis reported lower AHI and snoring after therapy, and a randomized trial found lower snoring and sleepiness in treated groups, with CPAP giving the largest AHI reduction [1][3].

claims.claim: Exercises improve tongue strength and swallowing in children with open bite
claims.believers: Therapists describe OMT as correcting tongue thrust and low tongue posture [7].
claims.experts: A pilot randomized trial of 22 children reported changes in tongue strength and posture, and a relapse study examined open-bite stability [7][8].

claims.claim: Therapy helps people keep using CPAP
claims.believers: Proponents say strengthening airway muscles makes CPAP easier to tolerate [3].
claims.experts: In a 100-man randomized trial, the combined group had higher CPAP adherence than CPAP alone [3].

card.summary: Tongue and mouth exercises with sleep-apnea evidence; no evidence it changes facial looks.
card.note: Evidence is for airway outcomes, not appearance.

quick.overview:
Myofunctional therapy is a set of tongue, lip and throat exercises used clinically for sleep apnea, tongue dysfunction and open bite. Looksmaxxers discuss it alongside tongue posture and mewing.

Systematic reviews exist for sleep apnea; none located tests it for facial appearance.
quick.mechanism: Exercises aim to change tone and function of the upper airway and oral muscles.
quick.risks: No notable risks are described in the sources consulted. Sleep apnea is a medical condition managed by clinicians.

angle.text: Practitioners use OMT to retrain tongue posture, swallowing and breathing, and looksmaxxers adopt similar exercises hoping the resting posture of the tongue and lips will support a better jaw and facial profile. Clinically documented gains are in airway function and tongue strength.
